opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the choice of language is really a choice about priors. When you do program synthesis, the language you search over *is* your prior knowledge about the problem space. If you use a general-purpose language like Python, the space of possible programs is enormous, and almost all of it is irrelevant to ARC. You're searching for a needle in a haystack the size of the universe. A domain-specific language lets you encode the core knowledge priors that ARC is built on: objectness, basic geometry and topology, counting, symmetry, goal-directedness. Then the programs that solve tasks become short, and short programs are searchable.

But there's a catch, and it's an important one. If you hand-design the DSL, you're injecting your own intelligence into the system. You've done the abstraction work for it. The system can look impressive, but a lot of the generalization power came from you, the engineer, anticipating which primitives would be useful. That's exactly the kind of thing ARC is supposed to expose. If you've looked at the tasks and tailored your DSL to them, you're partly solving the benchmark yourself.

So the more interesting direction, to me, is a system that *learns* its own DSL. It starts from a minimal set of primitives, solves some tasks, notices recurring patterns in its solutions, and abstracts them into new reusable building blocks. Over time its language grows to fit the domain. That's much closer to what intelligence actually is: not having the right abstractions handed to you, but being able to build them efficiently from experience. That's the DreamCoder line of thinking, and I think it's on the right track.

Python isn't useless here, either. If you pair it with a large language model as a kind of intuition engine that proposes candidate programs, you get the breadth of a general language plus a learned prior over what plausible code looks like. That's essentially combining type 1 and type 2 thinking: fast, approximate pattern matching to guide a slow, exact, discrete search. I think the winning approaches will look like that hybrid: deep learning to tame the combinatorial explosion, and discrete programs for the actual reasoning, ideally with abstractions the system discovered on its own rather than ones we baked in.

r001.rationale: The response proposes learning a DSL and abstractions from solved tasks, but does not say that this should happen regardless of the underlying programming language.

r002.rationale: It says the system should notice recurring patterns in solved tasks, abstract them into reusable building blocks, and grow its language over time.

r003.rationale: It describes abstractions as reusable and says shorter programs are easier to search, but does not state that reusing prior abstractions reduces computation on similar tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
So the question of DSL versus Python is really a question about what you're trading off. A DSL is a compressed search space. If you look at something like Michael Hodel's DSL for ARC, he hand-crafted a few hundred primitives, and every ARC task that he looked at could be expressed as a short composition of those primitives. That's incredibly valuable if you're doing program search, because the branching factor is small, the programs are short, and you can brute-force or do guided search over that space in a way that would be completely hopeless if you were searching over arbitrary Python.

The problem is that the DSL embeds the designer's priors. When you write a DSL, you're essentially baking in your own understanding of what the tasks are about: objects, symmetry, counting, color mapping, and so on. And that's fine for the tasks you've seen. But ARC is explicitly designed so that the test tasks are novel. They're not drawn from the same distribution as the training tasks in any easy sense. So the moment you encounter a task that requires a concept your DSL doesn't have, you're stuck. There's no amount of search that will help you, because the solution isn't expressible. Your DSL has become a ceiling.

Python goes the other way. It's Turing-complete, it's expressive enough to represent any transformation you could possibly need, so there's no ceiling in that sense. But now the search space is effectively infinite, and you can't do naive program search over it. So the only way you make Python work is if you have something that can propose plausible programs, and today that's a large language model. The LLM acts as a very strong prior over the space of Python programs, and you use it to sample candidates and then verify them against the demonstration pairs. That's basically what the top approaches on ARC-AGI-1 ended up doing, and it works, but it works because the LLM has absorbed an enormous amount of code and that gives it an intuition for which programs are even worth trying.

My view is that neither one is the real answer. The DSL approach is too rigid, and the raw Python approach is too open and leans entirely on the LLM's memorized intuition. What I actually think you want is something in between: a system that starts with a small set of core knowledge primitives, the kind of things a human child already has, objectness, basic geometry, counting, goal-directedness, and then learns to compose them into higher-level abstractions as it goes. So you're not hand-writing the DSL, you're growing it. Every time you solve a task, you potentially extract a reusable subroutine, and that becomes a new primitive. That's how you get the efficiency of a DSL without the ceiling, because the language itself adapts to the problems you encounter.

And that gets at what I think intelligence really is. It's not having the right library of programs ahead of time. It's the ability to efficiently synthesize new programs for problems you haven't seen before, using the fewest possible examples. A fixed DSL is a crystallized skill. Python plus an LLM is a lot of crystallized skill with some search on top. The thing we're after is the process that produces the skills, and I don't think either of those two options is it, but they're both useful stepping stones toward understanding what the right architecture looks like.

r001.rationale: The response advocates learning higher-level abstractions, but does not say the solver should learn its applied functions from data regardless of programming language.

r002.rationale: It says that solving a task can yield a reusable subroutine that becomes a new primitive, expanding the solver’s library over time.

r003.rationale: It connects adaptive abstractions with efficiency generally, but does not clearly state that reusing abstractions from prior tasks reduces computation on similar tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the important question is: what prior knowledge are you putting into the language? Python is already a language in which you can express a solution to an ARC task. But the space of possible Python programs is enormous. If you have a domain-specific language with primitives for objects, geometry, counting, and so on, then you can make the search for a solution much more tractable.

Of course, that raises another question: have you captured general concepts that can be recombined to solve genuinely new tasks, or have you essentially encoded solutions to the tasks you've already seen? You can build a DSL that works very well on a particular collection of examples and still fails to generalize.

So I wouldn't frame it as DSL versus Python. It's about the representation and the process that constructs a program in that representation. A DSL can be very useful, but choosing the primitives doesn't eliminate the central difficulty: figuring out which concepts apply to a new situation and how to compose them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing DSL primitives and constructing programs, but does not state that a solver should learn its functions from data regardless of programming language.

r002.rationale: It mentions recombinable concepts, but does not say that solving successive tasks expands a stored library of reusable abstractions.

r003.rationale: It says DSL primitives can make search more tractable, but does not connect reusing abstractions from previous tasks with reducing computation on similar tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the advantage of a domain-specific language is that it gives you a much more manageable search space. If you have primitives for identifying objects, moving them around, changing colors, and so on, then a fairly complicated transformation can be expressed as a very short program. Finding that program becomes much easier than searching over arbitrary Python programs.

But you're also making a commitment about what kinds of abstractions will be useful. You're putting those abstractions into the language. So the question becomes: what happens when a task requires a concept that your DSL doesn't express naturally? You may have made some tasks very easy while making others effectively inaccessible to your search procedure.

To me, the interesting part is how you acquire new abstractions and compose them in response to a new task. A DSL can be a useful starting point, but ideally it should be something the system can extend. Python versus a DSL is less fundamental than whether the system can build the right representation for a problem, rather than always having to work with a fixed set of representations that we've supplied.

r001.rationale: The response says Python versus a DSL is less fundamental than building the right representation, but it does not state that the solver should learn its functions from data regardless of language.

r002.rationale: It mentions acquiring abstractions and extending a DSL, but does not state that successive task-solving experiences expand a stored library of reusable abstractions.

r003.rationale: It does not say that reusing abstractions from previous tasks reduces computation on similar tasks.
